description: The job is slow but the GPU is idle: look at the host first. A GPU that is not busy is usually not being fed, and the feeding happens on the host. This dashboard walks one node's CPU, memory and NUMA, disk IO, network, InfiniBand and (opt-in) CPU memory bandwidth in USE order - utilization, saturation, errors - using node_exporter metrics only. Pair it with Algalon / GPU Utilization Quality for the GPU side of the same node.

links.title: Algalon dashboards
links.tooltip: Drill down into the fleet, queue and node views

panels.description: Reading order for this dashboard: sections run in USE order from the cheapest saturation signal (PSI) down to the opt-in memory-bandwidth panels.

options.content:
**When a training job is slow and its GPUs are idle, look at the host first.** Low GPU utilization means the GPU is not being fed. The feeding happens on the host: dataloader worker processes on the CPU, pinned host memory, the local disk or filesystem the dataset streams from, the Ethernet network, and the InfiniBand fabric that carries NCCL traffic between nodes. One of those is the bottleneck.

Read top to bottom, in USE order (Utilization, Saturation, Errors): **1. Saturation at a glance** (non-zero PSI names the starved resource) → **2. CPU** (is one core pegged while the average looks fine?) → **3. Memory and NUMA** (reclaim, swap, cross-socket allocations, OOM kills) → **4. Disk IO** (dataset reads and checkpoint writes) → **5. Network** (retransmits, drops, socket and conntrack limits) → **6. InfiniBand** (link state and error counters) → **7. CPU memory bandwidth** (opt-in, from resctrl).

Every panel is node_exporter data for the single node picked in `node`. For GPU-side evidence on the same node, open Algalon / GPU Utilization Quality; for alerting precursors, Algalon / Node Health (Precursors).

panels.title: Read this first: the job is slow but the GPU is idle

options.content:
### 1. Saturation at a glance
Pressure Stall Information: the share of wall time tasks lost waiting for a resource. Zero is healthy; a sustained non-zero line names the bottleneck.

panels.description:
Fraction of wall time in which at least one runnable task was waiting for a CPU. This is CPU saturation measured directly, not inferred from load average.

How to read: 0 is the healthy baseline. A sustained 0.1 or more means dataloader workers, the Python main loop or kernel threads are queueing for cores - the GPU is waiting on a CPU-bound input pipeline. Section 2 shows whether it is many cores or one.

PSI requires kernel 4.20+ with CONFIG_PSI and psi not disabled on the kernel command line (some distributions ship psi=0 by default, then pass psi=1). Empty when PSI is off.
panels.title: 1. CPU pressure (PSI some)

panels.description:
Fraction of wall time tasks stalled on memory: reclaim, swap-in, or refaulting evicted page cache. "some" means at least one task stalled; "full" means every non-idle task stalled at once, so the node did no useful work in that time.

How to read: any sustained "full" is serious - the dataloader and the training process are both frozen on memory. A non-zero "some" with "full" at 0 usually means the page cache holding the dataset is being evicted and re-read. Go to section 3.

PSI requires kernel 4.20+ with CONFIG_PSI and psi not disabled on the kernel command line (some distributions ship psi=0 by default, then pass psi=1). Empty when PSI is off.
panels.title: 1. Memory pressure (PSI some, full)

panels.description:
Fraction of wall time tasks stalled waiting for block IO. Covers local disks; IO to NFS or a parallel filesystem shows up here only partly, so read it together with Algalon / Checkpoint I/O for network storage.

How to read: "some" rising during the first minutes of a job is the dataset or checkpoint load and is expected. Sustained "some" during steady-state training means the input pipeline is reading from disk faster than the disk can serve it; "full" means the whole node is blocked on IO. Go to section 4.

PSI requires kernel 4.20+ with CONFIG_PSI and psi not disabled on the kernel command line (some distributions ship psi=0 by default, then pass psi=1). Empty when PSI is off.
panels.title: 1. IO pressure (PSI some, full)

panels.description:
1-minute load average divided by the number of logical CPUs. On Linux the load average counts runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (usually IO), so it mixes CPU and IO demand.

How to read: below 1.0 means there are idle CPUs on average. Above 1.0 means tasks are queueing for something - check CPU PSI and IO PSI above to tell which. Prefer PSI when it is available; this panel exists for kernels without it.
panels.title: 1. Load average per CPU

panels.description:
Share of CPU time not idle, averaged over every logical CPU (iowait counts as idle here, matching the kernel definition).

How to read: this is utilization, not saturation. A training node can sit at 30% average while one core is pegged and starving the GPU - the average hides it. Use it to spot a node that is busy overall, then use section 2 to find the hot core.
panels.title: 1. CPU utilization (all cores)

options.content:
### 2. CPU
Where CPU time goes, whether a single core is the bottleneck, and how long runnable tasks wait for a core.

panels.description:
Node-wide CPU time split by mode, as a share of all logical CPUs, stacked. Idle is left out, so the top of the stack is total busy time.

How to read: "user" is the training process and dataloader workers doing their job. High "system" points at the kernel - syscalls, page faults, network stack. "iowait" means CPUs idle with IO outstanding (section 4). "softirq" grows with packet rate (section 5). "steal" non-zero means the node is a VM and the hypervisor is taking cycles - a bare-metal node should never show it.
panels.title: 2. CPU time by mode

panels.description:
Utilization of the single busiest logical CPU, next to the node-wide average.

How to read: the gap between the two lines is the single-thread bottleneck. A busiest core pinned near 100% while the average is low means one thread - often the Python main loop, a single-process dataloader (num_workers=0), or one interrupt-handling core - is serializing the work that feeds the GPU. More cores will not help; more dataloader workers or better IRQ spreading will.
panels.title: 2. Busiest core vs average

panels.description:
Context switches per second across the node.

How to read: there is no universal good value - compare against this node's own history while the same job runs. A jump with no change in throughput usually means too many threads for the cores (for example, every dataloader worker also spawning a full OpenMP or BLAS thread pool) and the scheduler is thrashing between them.
panels.title: 2. Context switches

panels.description:
Instantaneous count of runnable tasks and of tasks blocked in uninterruptible sleep (D state, almost always waiting on IO).

How to read: "running" persistently above the CPU count means tasks are queueing for cores. "blocked" above zero for long stretches means processes are stuck on IO - a slow local disk or a hung network filesystem. A dataloader stuck on a hung NFS mount shows here before anywhere else.
panels.title: 2. Run queue: running and blocked tasks

panels.description:
Time runnable tasks spent waiting on a run queue for a CPU, summed over all CPUs, per second of wall time (from /proc/schedstat). The value reads as "on average, this many tasks were waiting for a core".

How to read: near 0 means a runnable task gets a core immediately. Values climbing toward the core count mean heavy CPU oversubscription. It moves with CPU PSI but counts every waiting task, not just whether any task waited.

Empty on kernels built without CONFIG_SCHEDSTATS.
panels.title: 2. Scheduler wait time

panels.description:
The eight logical CPUs that spend the largest share of time in hard and soft interrupt handling.

How to read: NIC and NVMe interrupts are often steered to a handful of cores. A core near 100% here is a packet- or IO-processing bottleneck that the node average hides; check irqbalance or the NIC's IRQ affinity. Read it with the softnet panel in section 5.
panels.title: 2. Interrupt and softirq time per core (top 8)

options.content:
### 3. Memory and NUMA
Host memory headroom, reclaim and swap activity, cross-socket allocations, and OOM kills.

panels.description:
MemAvailable (what the kernel estimates can be handed out without swapping), the page cache, and Shmem (tmpfs including /dev/shm, plus shared anonymous memory).

How to read: MemAvailable trending toward zero precedes reclaim and OOM kills. A shrinking page cache while a job streams its dataset means the dataset no longer fits in cache and every epoch rereads it from storage. Shmem grows with dataloader workers passing batches through /dev/shm and with NCCL shared-memory transport.
panels.title: 3. Available memory, page cache, shared memory

panels.description:
Size of the static HugePages pool and how much of it is free. Transparent huge pages are not counted here.

How to read: a pool of zero is normal unless the site reserves huge pages. When a pool is reserved, free near zero means jobs that expect huge pages fall back to normal pages; a large free pool is memory taken away from everything else.
panels.title: 3. HugePages (total, free)

panels.description:
Swap space in use (left axis) and pages swapped in and out per second (right axis).

How to read: swap in use that does not move is old cold pages and is harmless. Sustained swap-in during training is not harmless: the job is touching memory that was pushed to disk, and every such access stalls it. Read with memory PSI above.

Many GPU nodes run without swap; then all three lines sit at zero.
panels.title: 3. Swap: used and paging rate

panels.description:
Pages scanned and reclaimed per second, split into kswapd (background) and direct reclaim, plus major page faults.

How to read: kswapd scanning is the kernel tidying up in the background and is normal under a busy page cache. Direct reclaim is the expensive one - the allocating process itself (the training job, a dataloader worker) is made to free memory before it can continue. Major faults are reads from disk to satisfy a page access: a refaulting dataset, a memory-mapped file, or swap.
panels.title: 3. Page reclaim and major faults

panels.description:
Per NUMA node, pages per second: "miss" = allocated here although the process wanted another node, "foreign" = wanted here but allocated elsewhere, "other" = allocated here for a process running on another node.

How to read: on a two-socket GPU node each GPU and NIC hangs off one socket. A dataloader or pinned-memory buffer on the far socket sends every host-to-device copy across the socket interconnect. Sustained miss/foreign means memory placement does not follow the process - check the job's CPU and memory binding (--cpu-bind, numactl). The numaN in the legend is the NUMA node number: the exporter labels it "node", which the scrape renames to exported_node because "node" is the host name in Algalon.
panels.title: 3. NUMA misses, foreign and remote allocations

panels.description:
Free memory on each NUMA node as a share of that node's memory.

How to read: the nodes should drain roughly evenly. One node near zero while the other has room means allocations are piling onto one socket - the kernel will reclaim there or start allocating remotely (see the panel to the left) even though the machine as a whole has free memory.
panels.title: 3. Free memory per NUMA node

panels.description:
Processes killed by the kernel OOM killer, per 5 minutes.

How to read: any non-zero bar is an event worth a look. If it lines up with a job failure, the job died for host memory, not GPU memory. The kernel log names the process. A cgroup OOM inside a Slurm job allocation is counted here as well.

Requires kernel 4.13+ (the oom_kill vmstat field).
panels.title: 3. OOM kills

panels.description:
Data read from and written to block devices through the page cache, per second (pgpgin/pgpgout, in KiB as the kernel reports them).

How to read: page-in tracks dataset reads that miss the cache; page-out tracks dirty pages written back, mostly checkpoints. Page-out is also the signal behind the node-precursor alert rules - a node whose page-out leaves the fleet band is shown on Algalon / Node Health (Precursors).
panels.title: 3. Page-in and page-out rate

options.content:
### 4. Disk IO
Local block devices: how busy, how slow, how deep the queue, and how full the filesystems are.

panels.description:
Share of wall time each block device had at least one request in flight.

How to read: on a single spinning disk, near 100% means saturated. On NVMe and RAID devices that serve many requests in parallel, 100% only means "never idle" - use the queue depth and latency panels to judge saturation instead.
panels.title: 4. Disk busy time

panels.description:
Average time per completed request, queueing included, for reads and writes.

How to read: NVMe reads normally complete well under a millisecond. Read latency climbing while the job streams its dataset means the dataloader is waiting on the disk. Write latency spiking at checkpoint time is expected; spiking outside checkpoints is not.
panels.title: 4. Disk latency (await, read and write)

panels.description:
Bytes read and written per second per block device.

How to read: a read plateau that matches the device's rated bandwidth while GPUs idle is a disk-bound input pipeline - cache the dataset in memory, pre-shard it, or move it to faster storage. Write bursts at regular intervals are checkpoints.
panels.title: 4. Disk throughput

panels.description:
Average number of requests in flight (time-weighted) and the instantaneous count.

How to read: this is disk saturation. A queue that keeps growing while throughput stays flat means the device cannot take more - requests are just waiting longer. NVMe devices handle deep queues well; a queue persistently above a few on a SATA device is a bottleneck.
panels.title: 4. Disk queue depth

panels.description:
Free space as a share of size, per mounted filesystem (tmpfs and ramfs left out; /dev/shm has its own panel).

How to read: a filesystem near 0 fails checkpoint writes, log writes and the container runtime. Local scratch filling up across a job is the usual cause. Network filesystems mounted on the node appear here too and report the shared filesystem's free space, not this node's.
panels.title: 4. Filesystem free space

panels.description:
Bytes used in /dev/shm against its size.

How to read: PyTorch dataloader workers hand batches to the training process through /dev/shm, and NCCL uses it for intra-node transport. When it fills, jobs die with "Bus error" or "No space left on device" while ordinary memory still looks free. Used approaching size is the warning.

node_exporter skips mounts under /dev by default; Algalon's exporter flags re-include them so /dev/shm is collected.
panels.title: 4. /dev/shm usage

options.content:
### 5. Network
Ethernet and IPoIB interfaces (virtual and container interfaces left out), the TCP stack, and kernel table limits.

panels.description:
Bytes received and transmitted per second per physical interface.

How to read: compare against the link speed. A NIC running flat at its line rate while GPUs idle means the job is network-bound - typically data streaming from object storage or a network filesystem, or NCCL falling back to TCP sockets when it should be using InfiniBand (section 6 would then be quiet).
panels.title: 5. NIC throughput

panels.description:
Packets received and transmitted per second per physical interface.

How to read: a high packet rate with modest byte throughput means small packets, which costs CPU in softirq (section 2) rather than bandwidth. Compare with the throughput panel to tell the two apart.
panels.title: 5. NIC packet rate

panels.description:
Packets dropped and packets with errors per second, per interface and direction.

How to read: errors point at the physical layer - cable, optic, switch port. Drops on receive usually mean the host could not drain the ring buffer fast enough (see the softnet panel below). Healthy interfaces sit at zero.
panels.title: 5. NIC drops and errors

panels.description:
Retransmitted TCP segments as a share of all segments sent.

How to read: well under 1% is normal. Sustained values above that mean packet loss on the path, and TCP throughput collapses quickly with loss - storage reads and any TCP-based collective traffic slow down with it. Look for drops and errors on the left.
panels.title: 5. TCP retransmit ratio

panels.description:
Listen-queue overflows and drops, TCP timeouts and SYN retransmits, per second.

How to read: listen overflows and drops mean a server process on this node accepts connections more slowly than they arrive - a rendezvous or data-serving process under load. Timeouts and SYN retransmits mean peers are not answering, which during job start-up looks like a hang in distributed initialization.
panels.title: 5. TCP listen drops, timeouts and SYN retransmits

panels.description:
Kernel receive-path events per second, summed over CPUs: "dropped" = packets dropped because a CPU's backlog queue was full; "squeezed" = the receive softirq ran out of budget with work still pending.

How to read: both should be zero or close to it. Non-zero values mean the CPUs handling network receive cannot keep up with the packet rate - the drop happens in the host, not on the wire, so NIC counters can look clean. Spread receive queues over more cores (RSS, RPS) or raise netdev_budget.
panels.title: 5. softnet drops and squeezes

panels.description:
Connection-tracking table entries and allocated file descriptors, each as a share of its kernel limit.

How to read: either one reaching 100% makes new connections or file opens fail - conntrack exhaustion silently drops new connections, fd exhaustion fails opens with "Too many open files". A dataloader opening many small files, or many workers each holding connections, is the usual way a training node gets there. conntrack is empty when the nf_conntrack module is not loaded.
panels.title: 5. conntrack and file descriptor usage

panels.description:
Sockets in use node-wide, TCP sockets in use, and TCP sockets in TIME_WAIT.

How to read: a steadily climbing socket count during a job is a connection leak. Tens of thousands in TIME_WAIT means something opens and closes connections in a tight loop (for example, per-sample HTTP fetches from object storage) and can exhaust ephemeral ports.
panels.title: 5. Sockets in use

options.content:
### 6. InfiniBand
HCA ports carrying NCCL traffic between nodes. Every panel is empty on nodes without InfiniBand HCAs.

panels.description:
Data received and transmitted per second per HCA port (device:port).

How to read: during multi-node training the ports should carry steady, roughly symmetric traffic in step with the job's all-reduce cadence. One port much quieter than its peers means traffic is not spread across rails; all ports quiet while the job is running multi-node means NCCL is not using InfiniBand at all (check the Ethernet NIC panels).

Empty on nodes without InfiniBand HCAs (and on RoCE-only nodes whose adapters do not register under /sys/class/infiniband).
panels.title: 6. IB port throughput

panels.description:
Logical port state and physical port state (left axis), and the negotiated link rate (right axis).

How to read: a healthy port reads state 4 (ACTIVE) and physical state 5 (LinkUp). Anything else means the port is down or still training. A link rate below its peers means the link came up at reduced width or speed - a bad cable or optic, and a slow rail for every collective that crosses it.

Empty on nodes without InfiniBand HCAs (and on RoCE-only nodes whose adapters do not register under /sys/class/infiniband).
panels.title: 6. IB link state and rate

panels.description:
Link-level error counters per port, increase per 5 minutes: symbol errors, local link integrity errors, link-downed events and received packets with errors.

How to read: healthy ports stay at zero. A slow trickle of symbol errors is a marginal cable or optic that will get worse; link-downed events interrupt NCCL outright and usually line up with a job failure or a long collective timeout.

Empty on nodes without InfiniBand HCAs (and on RoCE-only nodes whose adapters do not register under /sys/class/infiniband).
panels.title: 6. IB link errors

panels.description:
Packets discarded on receive and transmit, and transmit-wait ticks (time the port had data to send but could not), per second.

How to read: transmit wait is fabric congestion seen from this port - the switch is not granting credits fast enough. It rises when many nodes converge on the same link. Discards mean packets were dropped because the port was down or congested. All of them should be near zero outside heavy all-to-all phases.

Empty on nodes without InfiniBand HCAs (and on RoCE-only nodes whose adapters do not register under /sys/class/infiniband).
panels.title: 6. IB discards and transmit wait

options.content:
### 7. CPU memory bandwidth (resctrl MBM, opt-in)
Bytes moved between each L3 domain (socket or die) and DRAM. Empty unless the resctrl MBM textfile export runs on this node.

panels.description: What the memory-bandwidth panels measure, why there is no 100% line, and what has to be installed on the node for them to show data.

options.content:
Memory bandwidth is the one host bottleneck the other sections cannot show: memory PSI and NUMA misses measure pressure and placement, not bandwidth, so a node can be bandwidth-bound while sections 1 and 3 look clean. A dataloader doing heavy CPU-side decoding and augmentation, or pinned-memory staging for many GPUs, can saturate it.

**There is no 100% line.** The platform's peak memory bandwidth is not exported, so compare a domain against this node's own history under the same job, or against a STREAM baseline measured on the same hardware. A flat plateau at the same value across jobs is the ceiling.

**Opt-in.** Empty unless resctrl is mounted on the node (CPU and kernel support for MBM required) and monitoring/exporters/resctrl-mbm-textfile.sh is scheduled to write into node_exporter's textfile directory. It reads the default resctrl monitor group only: whole node, per L3 domain, never per job - by design, to keep monitoring overhead near zero.

Without resctrl MBM, vendor PMU tools (Intel PCM, AMD uProf) measure per-socket memory bandwidth directly; they are not wired into Algalon.

panels.title: 7. How to read memory bandwidth

panels.description:
Whether the resctrl MBM textfile export ran on this node and could read MBM counters: 1 = available, 0 = the script ran but resctrl is not mounted or MBM is not readable. No value means the script is not scheduled on this node at all.

Opt-in: empty unless the operator mounted resctrl on the node and scheduled monitoring/exporters/resctrl-mbm-textfile.sh into node_exporter's textfile directory. It reads only the default resctrl monitor group, so it is per L3 domain for the whole node by design - there are no per-job groups, which keeps the monitoring overhead near zero.
panels.title: 7. MBM export available

panels.description:
Seconds since the resctrl MBM textfile export last ran on this node. The reference schedule is every 30 seconds; green under 2 minutes, orange under 10, red beyond - the bandwidth panels below are then showing stale counters, and a stale counter reads as zero bandwidth.

Opt-in: empty unless the operator mounted resctrl on the node and scheduled monitoring/exporters/resctrl-mbm-textfile.sh into node_exporter's textfile directory. It reads only the default resctrl monitor group, so it is per L3 domain for the whole node by design - there are no per-job groups, which keeps the monitoring overhead near zero.
panels.title: 7. MBM export age

panels.description:
Total memory traffic per L3 domain (one per socket, or per die on chiplet CPUs), bytes per second, from resctrl MBM total counters.

How to read: there is no 100% line - the platform's peak bandwidth is not exported. Compare against this node's own history or a STREAM baseline on the same hardware: a domain flat-topping near that baseline while GPUs idle is a memory-bandwidth-bound host. Two domains far apart under a symmetric job means the work is not spread over sockets.

Opt-in: empty unless the operator mounted resctrl on the node and scheduled monitoring/exporters/resctrl-mbm-textfile.sh into node_exporter's textfile directory. It reads only the default resctrl monitor group, so it is per L3 domain for the whole node by design - there are no per-job groups, which keeps the monitoring overhead near zero.
panels.title: 7. Memory bandwidth per L3 domain

panels.description:
Per L3 domain, the share of memory traffic not served from the domain's own NUMA node: 1 - local / total. Domains with no traffic in the window are left out rather than drawn as 0 or 100%.

How to read: near 0 means memory follows the CPUs that use it. High values mean cross-socket traffic, which costs both latency and interconnect bandwidth - read it with the NUMA misses panel in section 3, which says which allocations went remote.

Opt-in: empty unless the operator mounted resctrl on the node and scheduled monitoring/exporters/resctrl-mbm-textfile.sh into node_exporter's textfile directory. It reads only the default resctrl monitor group, so it is per L3 domain for the whole node by design - there are no per-job groups, which keeps the monitoring overhead near zero.
panels.title: 7. Remote (cross-NUMA) share of memory traffic

title: Algalon / Host Saturation (USE)
